Post-test inspection of the reformer (Figure 11) revealed carbon deposition on the inner electrode surfaces, confirming methane decomposition into solid carbon and hydrogen via CH → C + 2H 4 2 (route 1). However, the detection of C H (Figure 10), indicated that some methane decomposition 2 2 also proceeded through a secondary pathway: 2CH → C H + 3H (route 2). The image 4 2 2 2 comparison highlights differences in carbon accumulation between low and high frequency operation, suggesting that higher frequency operation (100 kHz) favors route 1, while lower frequency conditions (10 kHz) preferentially drive route 2. The carbon buildup was readily removable, indicating that deposition occurred primarily through gas-phase condensation rather than surface-catalyzed mechanisms. Overall, the bench-scale tests validated both the electrical and chemical design principles of the plasma reformer. Stable plasma generation and energy efficient methane conversion were achieved across multiple operating conditions. These findings established a solid foundation for subsequent high-flow facility testing and engine integration phases. Figure 11 intentionally omitted from public version. Post-test inspection of the plasma reformer confirmed the presence of solid carbon residue following plasma operation, consistent with partial methane decomposition under non-thermal plasma conditions. Carbon accumulation increased with higher operating frequency, as expected from enhanced methane conversion rates, but remained manageable and did not impair reformer operation. These observations support the proposed plasma-chemical reaction pathways responsible for methane decomposition. Figure 11. Photographs of reactor internal components following plasma operation. Southwest Research Institute® U.S. DOE Award Number DE-FE0032301 Public Version - 9 - DE-FE0032301 Final Report 3.3 High-Flow Facility Testing Following successful bench-scale validation, high-flow testing was conducted at SwRI’s MRF to evaluate the plasma reformer under engine-scale gas flow conditions. The MRF provides a closed- loop natural-gas system capable of delivering precisely controlled flow rates up to 500 SLPM and pressures up to 60 psig, simulating the fuel delivery conditions expected for large-bore engine operation. The reformer, analytical instrumentation, and flow-conditioning equipment were installed outdoors on a dedicated test pad to ensure safety and controlled handling of the high-pressure methane flow. Figure 12 provides an overview of the MRF site and the specific reformer test setup. Figure 12. Overview of the SwRI MRF and high-flow reformer test setup. The right image shows the reformer installation area, including the flow-conditioning system, plasma reactor, and downstream mass spectrometer used for gas analysis. Testing covered a range of flow conditions between 50 and 500 SLPM and pressures from 10 to 30 psig. Stable plasma ignition and operation were consistently achieved for flow rates up to approximately 300 SLPM.
